title: The Bus
synopsis: Vera Moll is seventeen, leaving the Iowa farm town where her mother died, riding a Pulse-feeder coach east toward GLMZ refugee intake with a toolkit that was her mother's, a pair of boots that don't fit yet, and a borrowed pair of earbuds that work in one ear. A Vietnamese-Black field medic two seats up notices the toolkit and gives her three things: a name for what she is, a clean diagnostic clip, and the address of a corner building where the landlord doesn't ask questions.
characters: Auntie Hoa (transient — Vietnamese-Black field medic on the bus)
html:
# The Bus

The Behemoth was watching the bus pull out.

Vera knew it wasn't watching, technically. Iowan Behemoths didn't have eyes the way people meant *eyes* — they had pressure plates and ambient sensors and the long indifferent attention of a thing built to tend cornfields. But the autonom had risen up on its forward struts when the bus engaged the magnetic feeder line, and its dish-array had tilted toward the east, and Vera's neighbor Mrs. Kowalski-Obeng would have called that *minding*, and Mrs. Kowalski-Obeng was usually right about things that didn't need to be right.

*It's not minding,* Vera thought. *It's minding the field.*

The field was minded. The bus pulled out anyway.

She had the window seat, third row, pressed against the glass because the glass was the coolest surface within reach and she had not slept in two nights and wanted something to put her cheek on that wasn't her own arm. Outside: rows. Corn at second-cycle yellow, soy at meridian green, the irrigation drip-lines glinting where the early sun caught them. The Behemoth shrank into a comma against the horizon. Then a period. Then nothing the eye could resolve from a moving bus.

She didn't cry. She had decided not to cry forty miles back, when the bus had turned onto the corridor and the last familiar silo had passed behind her, and a decision once made was a decision. *You can renegotiate after the next stop,* she told herself, which was what her mother used to say about hard things, and which had nothing to do with not crying and everything to do with continuing to function, and was therefore exactly the right thing.

In her lap: the canvas roll. Inside the canvas roll: her mother's tools.

Not all of them. The cardiac kit had stayed with the cousin who had a cardiac client. The sutures had stayed with the clinic at the township line, because the clinic at the township line still had patients and Vera, at seventeen, did not yet. What she had taken were the diagnostic instruments — the calibrators, the hand probes, the small bone-handled set with the brass fittings that her mother had used to scrape gunk off of contact pads since before Vera could remember. The set had a leather band that snapped closed with a satisfying *click* and it was the most expensive thing Vera owned and she was carrying it across what had been Missouri once, what was now mostly water, and would arrive in GLMZ before sundown with it still snapped shut against her thigh.

Also in her lap: the boots, off her feet, because the boots did not fit yet. Black steel-toed, scuffed at the toe to a glint of underlayer, repaired at the sole twice already. They had been her mother's. Her mother had been five-eight. Vera was — five-foot-nothing, five-foot-and-an-attitude — and her feet had not yet decided what they were going to be. Walking in the boots was like walking in good shelter. You wore the shelter until you grew into it. *Eventually,* she thought, *the leather will know me.* She was prepared to wait.

The earbuds were in her ears, but only the left one worked. The right side had cracked at the connector somewhere around hour fourteen and she was going to fix it at her next stable seat, which was not this one. The left earbud was playing what she had loaded onto the chip before leaving — eight hours of music she had pulled off old town-network archives, badly compressed, full of clicks where the encoding had failed, and she had decided the clicks were percussion.

One of the songs was an old American song from before the Centennial. Acoustic guitar, woman singing, lyrics about a road. Vera couldn't remember whose road it had been. She remembered her mother humming the chorus once, in the small kitchen in the small house, while she had made coffee on a small stove. Vera, eleven, had been at the table doing arithmetic. Her mother had been at the stove. The smell of coffee and the hum and the morning light on the linoleum.

The song played. Vera looked at the cornfields.

*Hi, Mom,* she thought. *I'm leaving now. I know you know.*

The woman two seats ahead of her had been watching the toolkit.

Vera felt it the way you feel a slight thumb of pressure on the back of your neck when someone in a room has decided to attend to you. The woman was older — fifty, maybe, dark-skinned with a deeper undertone of red where the bus light caught her cheekbone, hair cut close to her skull and silvered at the temples. She had been reading something on a paper-thin reader and her eyes had drifted left, then sharpened, then rested on the canvas roll. Vera felt her mother's tools become visible.

She started to slide the roll behind her bag.

"Don't," the woman said. Quiet. Not mean. "I'm not going to take it."

Vera stopped sliding.

"That's a field medic's roll," the woman said. "Pre-corp. Mid-century leather. The brass fittings on a Reisman set. I haven't seen one of those in fifteen years."

"It was my mother's."

The woman's face did the thing faces do when they have already understood the next sentence before the speaker has reached it. She did not say *I'm sorry*. Vera was grateful. She had decided, three months ago, that she was going to find people who didn't say it and stay near them.

"Where you headed," the woman said.

"Refugee processing at the East Pulse Hub. Then — I don't know. They give you a list."

"They give you a list," the woman agreed, with the small private smile of someone who had once been given a list. "Listen. The list is real but it isn't the whole map. You go to the East Hub, you process, you take the bunk for the night because the bunk is free and you need sleep more than you need pride. In the morning you don't take the list housing. You take the West Town transit. You get off at Ashland and Chicago. You walk to the corner building with the cream brick, the rounded face, the two addresses on the front."

"Two addresses?"

"Two addresses. Either is real. Neither is complete. The landlord likes that. He'll like you because you have those tools and you know what they do, and because you're scared in a way that he'll recognize as serviceable. He doesn't take credits the first month. He takes a favor he'll name later, and you'll do it, and the favor will be reasonable. After that it's two-fifty Quanta, paid in person, paid late if you have to but paid."

Vera was writing it down. She wrote on the inside of her left forearm with a thin marker because notebooks attracted attention and forearms didn't. *Ashland. Chicago. Cream brick. Rounded.*

"What's the building called."

"It's not called anything. The people who live there call it The Pivot."

"The Pivot."

"You're going to need a name to give the landlord," the woman said, "that isn't on your refugee paperwork. I'd suggest something short. Something that sounds like a tool, because you carry tools, and people remember names that match the bag they came in."

Vera looked at her toolkit. She looked at the cornfields, going.

"Pixel," she said. It came out without thinking, the way a name does when it's been waiting.

"Pixel." The woman tried it. "Yes. That'll work."

She reached into her own bag. Vera tensed — not in fear, in the small electric way you tense when a stranger reaches for something on your behalf. The woman pulled out a small flat package, thin foil, sealed.

"Diagnostic clip," the woman said. "Sterile. Civilian-grade but the brand is good. You won't have time to sterilize anything when you start working again, and you will start working again. Take it."

"I don't have anything to —"

"You don't owe me anything. I owed someone else this when I was your age. They didn't take payment either." She put the foil packet on Vera's tray. "My name is Hoa. If you need a name for someone who told you about The Pivot, it isn't mine. Use *Auntie*. The landlord will know who you mean."

Vera looked at the foil packet on the tray. It caught the bus light. It looked, in that light, exactly like the kind of thing her mother used to slip into her pocket on rounds — a small clean instrument waiting for the moment it would be needed.

She wrote it down. *Auntie Hoa.*

Then she crossed it out, because Hoa had said not to use her name, and wrote *Auntie* instead, and then she put the marker away and put the packet in the canvas roll and snapped the roll closed with the satisfying *click*.

The bus rolled east.

The left earbud was still playing. The song had moved on to something else, something Vera didn't recognize but liked anyway, a thing with a fast slipping bassline that the encoding clicks made into percussion.

She pressed her cheek against the cool window. She watched the world that was no longer hers slide past. She thought, with the small clear surprise that would later become a habit:

*I am not actually doing this badly.*

The Behemoth was long gone behind her, minding its field. The boots were heavy in her lap. The tools were quiet. The packet was new.

She was, she realized, a person with three things now. A name that fit the bag. A list, and the route around the list. And one packet of clean foil from a stranger who hadn't asked for thanks.

*Pixel,* she practiced, in the privacy of her own head.

It sounded like something.

It sounded like *her*.
